meaning: Hawaiian deity, associated with fertility, agriculture, rainfall, music and peace

phonemes.desc: Voiced alveolar lateral [l] plus open-mid back [o]; Hawaiian stress falls on the first syllable of the name.
Voiced alveolar nasal [n] plus open-mid back [o]; Hawaiian vowels are pure and every syllable is fully sounded.

pronunciation.approximation: 'LOH-noh' — two clean open syllables, the weight on the first; no diphthong, no swallowed ending.

kin.label: Pan-Polynesian
kin.form: Rongo — the same theonym across the eastern Pacific: Māori Rongo (god of the kūmara and of peace), Marquesan ʻOno, Tahitian Roʻo, Rarotongan Rongo (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology ch. 4; Craig, Dictionary of Polynesian Mythology s.v. Rongo).

kin.label: Hawaiian lexicon
kin.form: lono — the ordinary noun 'news, tidings, report, fame'; the god's name is the word for tidings made divine (Pukui & Elbert, Hawaiian Dictionary s.v. lono).

kin.label: Sound change
kin.form: Proto-Polynesian *R → Hawaiian l: *Rongo becomes Lono by the regular consonant shift that Hawaiianized the old god's name.

pronunciation.note: Lono is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Hawaiian name is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter. Nor is there an older spelling for Unicode to recover: Hawaiian was unwritten until mission scribes fixed the alphabet in the 1820s. The restoration honors the name as the pan-Polynesian Rongo's Hawaiian form.

domains.title: Lono
domains.subtitle: Agriculture
domains.lead: Lono is the Hawaiian god of fertility, agriculture, rainfall, music, and peace — the deity of the Makahiki season, when war was forbidden and the feathered image of the long god made its circuit of every island collecting tribute. His name is the ordinary Hawaiian word for news and tidings, as if the arriving god were good news himself.

cards.name: The Makahiki Circuit
cards.desc: The akua loa — the long, feathered image of Lono — was carried counterclockwise around each island for four months of peace, games, and tribute (Malo, Hawaiian Antiquities, ch. 33).

cards.name: Rain and Cultivation
cards.desc: His cloudburst watered the dry leeward fields; under his star the people planted ʻuala, sweet potato, and the year turned from war to husbandry.

cards.name: The Peace of Lono
cards.desc: During Lono's months the temples closed to war and the aliʻi gathered the Makahiki tax — a season when law was the god's own itinerary.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Preserved as a flagship temple; a pre-literate name first written by mission scribes in the 1820s, restored here to Polynesian dignity.

symbols.name: The akua Lono
symbols.meaning: The long feathered image carried around the island in the Makahiki circuit — the god made portable, travelling to receive his tribute.

symbols.name: The Pleiades (Makaliʻi)
symbols.meaning: Whose heliacal rising opened the Makahiki season — Lono returned with the star-cluster the sailors also steered by.

symbols.name: Rain over the leeward fields
symbols.meaning: His cloudburst on the dry Kona side of the islands — the storm that answered drought and began the planting year.

symbols.name: The sweet potato (ʻuala)
symbols.meaning: The dryland crop of Lono's months, planted as the god came round — agriculture performed as liturgy.

symbols.name: The sacrificial pig (puaʻa)
symbols.meaning: The offering laid at each ahupuaʻa boundary platform as the image passed — the tax paid in flesh to the god of peace.

mythology.lead: Lono's stories are Hawaiʻi's seasonal memory: a chief who lost his wife and sailed away to Kahiki promising return, and a god who returns every year as the Makahiki — the months when rain, games, and taxation replace war. When Cook sailed into Kealakekua Bay during the festival, the myth was already waiting for him.

myths.title: Lono and Kaikilani
myths.text: Among the chiefly legends preserved by Kamakau and Beckwith, Lono-i-ka-makahiki is a chief of Kaʻawaloa in the Kona district of Hawaiʻi island, whose story became the god's. His wife is the beautiful Kaikilani; a jealous rival fabricates reports of her infidelity, and Lono — believing the lie — kills her, learning the truth too late (Kamakau, Ruling Chiefs of Hawaiʻi). Maddened by grief, he wanders the island, boxing and wrestling his way around the coast, until he boards a canoe at Kealakekua and sails for Kahiki, promising to return. The people say the Makahiki is that return: the god comes back each year when the Pleiades rise, and the season of his circuit is the season of peace. Beckwith's variant (Hawaiian Mythology, ch. 15) reshapes the tale within Pele's circle — a reminder that the legend grew in more than one telling, and that its fixed point is the departure and the promise, not any single version of the crime.

myths.title: The Circuit of the Long God
myths.text: The Makahiki, the Hawaiian New Year festival, is Lono's season and his biography performed. When the Pleiades (Makaliʻi) appeared at sunset, the temples closed to war and the image of the long god (akua loa) — a tall staff hung with feathered emblems — was carried around each island counterclockwise, district by district (Malo, Hawaiian Antiquities, ch. 33; Kamakau, The Works of the People of Old). At every ahupuaʻa boundary the procession halted at the ahu platform, where a pig was offered and the ruling chief's collectors gathered the Makahiki tribute, the hoʻokupu that funded the court's year. Boxing, surfing, and spear-dancing filled the days, and ordinary disputes were set aside until the god had passed. For four months, taxation itself was liturgy: the god circled the land, and the land's wealth circled with him. When the image was lifted back into the temple at the season's end, war could resume — the myth's own answer to what holds a kingdom together when no enemy threatens.

myths.title: The God Who Sails In
myths.text: On 17 January 1779, in the middle of the Makahiki season, James Cook sailed into Kealakekua Bay, and Hawaiians had a story already shaped for him. Priests conducted the white stranger to the great heiau of Hikiau as Lono makua returned from Kahiki; offerings were laid before him, he was anointed, and the British spent a month in the god's retinue — an identification the expedition's journals record with visible discomfort (Cook, ed. Beaglehole; Kamakau, Ruling Chiefs of Hawaiʻi). Whether the Hawaiians truly believed Cook was Lono, or were performing the season's own grammar upon an arrival, remains the famous dispute: Sahlins reads the reception as structurally exact, Obeyesekere as European myth-making projected onto the scene. Either way the episode shows a myth acting in real time — an arrival rehearsed in ceremony for a thousand years, at last keeping its appointment.

myths.title: The Death of the God at Kealakekua
myths.text: When Cook returned to Kealakekua in February 1779 with a broken mast, the season had turned and the bay was crowded; a cutter was stolen from the Discovery, and in the quarrel that followed Cook was struck down on the beach at Kaʻawaloa on 14 February. The god had been killed — and the sources disagree about what that meant. Sahlins argues the death completed the Makahiki's logic: the god arrives, is honored, and departs violently, and Cook's remains, divided among the chiefs, became relics rather than a corpse. Obeyesekere denies the apotheosis entirely. Kamakau's account is cooler: the chief Kalaniʻōpuʻu treated the body as that of a great chief, and the bones were eventually returned. Whatever happened on the beach, the myth had ended as the season ends — with the god gone and the people expecting him back.

lore.syncretism: Across Polynesia, Lono's kin rule the cultivated foods: Māori Rongo — hidden guardian of the kūmara and god of peace, one of the children of Rangi and Papa — Marquesan ʻOno, Tahitian Roʻo, and Rarotongan Rongo are all reflexes of the same eastern-Pacific theonym whose Hawaiian form arrives by the regular sound change (Beckwith, ch. 4; Craig, s.v. Rongo). In Aotearoa, Rongo is invoked to make peace; in Hawaiʻi, Lono's four months did the same work. The mission century overlaid the pattern: Christian preachers found in Lono's annual return a ready-made parable of the second coming, and Hawaiian converts could hear the Makahiki itself as prophecy. Modern scholarship has made Lono a battleground of another kind — the Sahlins–Obeyesekere debate over Cook's apotheosis is, at bottom, a debate over whether gods can still walk in when the calendar says they should.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Makahiki never fully died. In the Hawaiian renaissance that began in the 1970s it returned as school festivals, games leagues, and island-wide circuits of the akua images; today Hawaiian immersion schools open their year with it, and the festival's sports — wrestling, surfing, spear-throwing — have league lives of their own. Kealakekua Bay is a state historical park, and a white obelisk at Kaʻawaloa marks where the god-story and the captain's log collided. In 1976 the voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa made Lono's return literal, sailing to Tahiti and back by traditional navigation — Kahiki proven reachable, the promise kept by human hands. Lono remains a common Hawaiian given name, and the god's peace still names the season when a year, not a war, can begin.
lore.extendedMeditation: Lono is the god who comes back — and that is nearly the whole of him. He does not rule from a fixed temple; he arrives, stays four months, and leaves, and the year is built around his absence as much as his presence. In this he is almost unique among the great gods of the world: a deity whose defining quality is returnability. When Cook sailed in during the Makahiki, the Hawaiians did not need to invent anything. Myth had already written the scene: the god lands from across the sea, is received by the chiefs and priests, and then — the season being over — is let go. It is among the most honest creations any people made of their relationship with power: the blessings arrive seasonally, the taxes are gathered religiously, and the god, like rain, is trusted because he has always come back before. To live under Lono is to live in a world where peace has a schedule, and where hope is not optimism but calendrical fact.

Sahlins, Marshall, Historical Metaphors and Mythical Realities (1981); Obeyesekere, Gananath, The Apotheosis of Captain Cook (1992)
lore.archaeology: The material trace of Lono is the Makahiki landscape itself. Hikiau heiau at Kealakekua Bay — the platform where Cook was received as the returned god — survives as a restored temple complex above the bay, beside the older Mailekini heiau, while the Cook monument obelisk stands at Kaʻawaloa across the water. Along the old circuits, ahu — small offering platforms at ahupuaʻa boundaries — mark where the akua image halted and the tribute was laid. No pre-contact temple can be securely assigned to Lono alone: Hawaiian heiau served shifting dedications, and his worship was mobile by design, carried around the island on poles rather than fixed in stone. The archaeology is therefore the route, not the shrine — a procession that left platforms every few miles around every inhabited island.
lore.originalScriptNote: Hawaiian was an unwritten language until the 1820s, when mission scribes fixed the alphabet, so the name has no older orthography for Unicode to recover — Lono is itself the first spelling. The philological record is the sound change instead: pan-Polynesian *Rongo becomes Hawaiian Lono by the regular shift of *R to l, with the second *g dropping, leaving a name that Hawaiian speakers heard as both the ancient god and their own word for tidings.
